summary: Describes APEX, an extensible, asynchronous message relaying service for application layer programs. It provides a best-effort application-level delivery mesh that other services build on. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: APEX is a way for one program to send a message to another program over the network. The message travels through servers that forward it to the destination, and each program signs in as a named endpoint first.

questions: what is the application exchange core
subtitle: An extensible messaging service that lets applications exchange data through a relaying mesh.

tldr.problem: Applications need a common way to pass messages to one another, with delivery semantics they can vary, without every application building its own transport.
tldr.mechanism: APEX defines a best-effort datagram service over BEEP. An application attaches to the relaying mesh as a named endpoint, sends data elements naming an originator and one or more recipients, and may attach options that change how relays process the message.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was a Standards Track document from July 2002 and is now Historic. The security section requires the BEEP DIGEST-MD5 profile for authentication and the BEEP TLS profile for confidentiality in every implementation.

today: RFC 3340 is a Historic RFC from July 2002. It specified an Internet standards track protocol at the time, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its security section requires every implementation to support the BEEP DIGEST-MD5 profile for authentication and the BEEP TLS profile for confidentiality.

sections.title: What APEX Is For
sections.content:
APEX, the Application Exchange, is an extensible, asynchronous message relaying service for application layer programs. At its core it provides a best-effort datagram service. Each datagram, simply termed data, is originated and received by APEX endpoints, which are applications that dynamically attach to the APEX relaying mesh. The data transmitted specifies an originating endpoint, an opaque content given by a URI reference, one or more recipient endpoints, and zero or more options.

The RFC starts from the observation that network applications differ along five operational characteristics: server push or client pull, synchronous or asynchronous, time-assured or time-insensitive, best-effort or reliable, and stateful or stateless. The world-wide web is a pull, synchronous, time-insensitive, reliable, stateless service, while Internet mail is a push, asynchronous, time-insensitive, best-effort service without delivery status notification, and stateless. Messaging applications vary considerably in their operational requirements, and these features come at a cost in both infrastructural and configuration complexity, so the underlying service must be extensible to support different requirements in a consistent manner. The core service supports a range of operational characteristics and a variety of tailored services for both user-based and programmatic exchanges.

APEX is specified in part as a BEEP profile, so many aspects of APEX, such as authentication, are provided within the BEEP core. Additional APEX services are provided on top of the relaying mesh, for example access control and presence information.
sections.plainLanguage: APEX is a way for one program to send a message to another program over the network. The message travels through servers that forward it to the destination, and each program signs in as a named endpoint first.

sections.title: Endpoints, Relays and the Relaying Mesh
sections.content:
APEX has two kinds of participant. An endpoint is an application that attaches to the relaying mesh and sends or receives data. A relay is a server that forwards data between endpoints, and relays act on behalf of administrative domains. An APEX process is either an application attached as an APEX endpoint or an APEX relay. APEX runs over BEEP, which runs over TCP.

APEX is used in two modes. In endpoint-relay mode the endpoint is always the BEEP initiator of the service and relays are always the BEEP listeners; applications attach as endpoints and then the transmission of data occurs. In relay-relay mode relays typically, though not necessarily, reside in different administrative domains; applications bind as relays and then the transmission of data occurs.

Relaying between administrative domains is configured using SRV resource records, so the actual number of relays between two endpoints is not fixed. The address of a relay for an administrative domain is found with the SRV algorithm, using the service name apex-edge for the endpoint-relay mode or apex-mesh for the relay-relay mode, the protocol tcp, and the administrative domain itself.
sections.plainLanguage: An application attaches to a relay and gives it a name. The relay forwards data to other relays, and each relay hands the data to the application it is addressed to.

sections.title: Naming Endpoints and Relays
sections.content:
Endpoints are named with an address, an at sign and a domain, written as local at Domain, where the local part is a token and may be followed by a slash and a subaddress. Two conventions apply to that syntax. Endpoint identities whose local part starts with apex= are reserved for use by APEX services registered with IANA. A solidus in the local part identifies a subaddress of an endpoint identity, so fred/appl=wb@example.com is a subaddress of the APEX endpoint fred@example.com, and subaddresses starting with appl= are reserved for APEX endpoint applications registered with IANA.

Relays are not named, but serve on behalf of administrative domains, which are identified by a fully qualified domain name or a domain literal such as [10.0.0.1]. Because the local part of an entity is a string of UTF-8 octets, comparison operations on it use exact matching and are case-sensitive, so fred@example.com and Fred@example.com refer to different endpoints, although a relay serving the example.com administrative domain may choose to treat the two endpoints identically for routing and delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: Each program has a name that looks like an email address, such as fred@example.com. A name with a slash marks a sub-part of the same program, so different parts of one application can use the same account.

sections.title: The Four Operations
sections.content:
An application attaches to the relaying mesh with an attach element that names the endpoint it wants to attach as and carries a transaction identifier. The relay checks the transaction identifier, the administrative domain, and whether the application is authorized for that endpoint; if another application has already attached as the same endpoint it refuses, and otherwise it binds the application and returns an ok element. A relay that wants to identify itself as a relay sends a bind element naming the administrative domain it serves, and the terminate operation releases an attachment or a binding. Failures come back as an error element with a numeric code, such as 537 for an action not authorized for the user, 553 for a parameter invalid, 554 for a transaction failed and 555 for a transaction already in progress.

Data travels in a data element, which names the content with a URI reference, the originating endpoint, one or more recipient endpoints, and any options. Each payload exchanged via APEX consists of an XML document and possibly an arbitrary MIME content. If only XML is sent the mapping to a BEEP payload is straightforward; if an arbitrary MIME content is present it is included in the payload as a multipart/related part identified with a cid URL, and the XML control document points at it.

When a relay receives a data element it checks that the sender is allowed to originate data on behalf of the stated originator, processes any per-data options, returns an ok element, and then processes per-originator options. For each recipient it processes any per-recipient options. If the recipient endpoint is in another administrative domain, the relay opens an APEX session to a relay that accepts data for that domain and sends a new data element there. If the recipient is in the same administrative domain, the APEX access service checks that the originator is allowed to communicate with the recipient, the recipient endpoint must currently be attached, and a new data element containing only that recipient is sent to the application. Relays are expressly forbidden from modifying the content of the data element at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: Four messages do the work: attach, bind, terminate and data. A data message names who sent it, who should get it and where the content is.

sections.title: Options That Change the Service
sections.content:
APEX provides a best-effort datagram service at its core, and options are used to alter the semantics of that service. An option element sits inside a data, originator, recipient or attach element. The internal or external attribute identifies the option, targetHop specifies which relays should process it, mustUnderstand specifies whether an unrecognized option must cause an error in processing, transID gives the option a transaction identifier, and localize can name a preferred language for textual diagnostics returned to the originator.

The targetHop attribute has three values. this means the option applies to this relay and must be removed before the containing element is transmitted. final means it applies to this relay only if the relay will transmit the containing element directly to the recipient, and a final relay does not remove options as it transmits. all means the option applies to this relay and is retained for the next one.

The core RFC defines one option, statusRequest, which asks each applicable relay to send a status response back to the originator. It must not appear in any data operation that carries a status response, because applications should avoid looping behaviour if an option is received in error. Other options are registered with IANA, and that is what makes the service extensible without changing the core protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: An option is a small instruction attached to a message, such as asking for a delivery report. The sender can say which relay should act on it and whether a relay that does not understand it should refuse the message.

sections.title: Authentication, Authorization and Confidentiality
sections.content:
Authentication, authorization and confidentiality are all matters of provisioning for each BEEP peer. A relay may be provisioned to let a BEEP peer identity coincide with a given endpoint identity, so a peer that authenticates as fred@example.com is allowed to attach as the endpoint fred@example.com, and the subaddress convention extends that to the subaddresses of that endpoint. A relay typically requires its BEEP peer to authenticate as a prelude to authorization, although an endpoint usually does not require the same of its peer. Access to APEX comes from three things together: authenticating as a BEEP peer, attaching as an endpoint or binding as a relay, and being listed as an actor by the APEX access service.

Data considered sensitive by an originating endpoint has its content encrypted for the intended recipients rather than relying on hop-by-hop encryption, and the endpoint signs the content when end-to-end authentication is wanted. Relays forward the opaque content unchanged, so the application is responsible for protecting it, and MIME-based security services such as OpenPGP or S/MIME may be used for that. All APEX implementations must provide the BEEP SASL DIGEST-MD5 profile for authentication and the BEEP TLS profile for confidentiality, using the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher, and a profile that supports client-side certificates for both. The RFC also warns that the statusRequest option may expose private network topology, so an administrator may wish to disable it except at the ingress and egress points of the administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The servers decide who may use which name, and the sending program is responsible for encrypting anything private. The service requires servers to support a standard way of checking passwords and a standard way of encrypting the connection.
